---
title: "Bayesian Genotyping"
subtitle: "`r paste0('Dataset: ', params$dataset_name)`"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_float: true
    toc_depth: 2
    number_sections: true
    code_folding: hide
    df_print: kable
    highlight: tango
    theme:
      version: 5
      bg: "#FFFFFF"
      fg: "#2E2A26"
      primary: "#657359"
      secondary: "#8B775F"
      base_font: "Times New Roman"
      heading_font: "Times New Roman"
      headings-font-weight: 700
      code_font:
        google: "JetBrains Mono"
date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%d %B %Y')`"
params:
  # Dataset
  dataset_name: "big" # or "big"
  n_cores: 4 # number of cores

  # Primer panel path
  primer_panel_path: "Data/Supporting_data/Primer_panels/12864_2021_7761_MOESM12_ESM_filtered.xlsx"

  # What to run
  run_stan: TRUE # runs Bayes model
  run_downsampling: TRUE # runs downsampling and calibration statistics (needs run_stan: TRUE in the same run)
  run_downsampling_plots: TRUE # runs visualisations (from this run, or from the saved run with the same settings)
  
  # Input reads and primers settings
  input_type: "unpadded" # "padded" or "unpadded"
  use_anchors: true
  anchor_length: 3
  probe_type: "asp_primers" # "asp_primers" or "reference"
  threshold_type: "errors" # "fraction" or "errors"
  min_score_fraction: 0.65 # "fraction" only
  error_rate: 0.08 # "errors" only

  # Inputs for call_genotype() function
  minimum_required_depth: 3 # minimum reads required to accept it for further genotyping
  HT_min_frequence: 0.20 # minor allele must be larger or equal to call HT

  # Inputs for strand check filter or flag
  strand_flag_prob: 0.01 # strand check, a direction needs at least 8 reads before its flagged
  expected_minor_fraction: 0.44 # derived from data (or 0.5)
  strand_downgrade: false # false = strand check only flags it, true = HT is changed to HM

  # Genotype prior
  prior_type: "ancestry" # "flat" = 1/3 each genotype, "het_share" = one heterozygote share for every pair, "hwe" = locus specific HWE priors from the primer panel
  prior_het_share: 0.15 # only for prior_type = "het_share": prior probability of a heterozygote (the two homozygotes share the rest)
  prior_population: "FreqWOLF_all" # only used when prior_type == "hwe": FreqWOLF_all, FreqWOLF_EastEurope, FreqWOLF_IT, FreqWOLF_IB, FreqDOG
  prior_floor: 0.001 # floors for allele frequency
  ancestry_prior_shape: 1 # only for prior_type = "ancestry": Beta(shape, shape) prior on wolf ancestry, 1 = uniform, 0.5 = leans to pure animals
  phi_hom_structure: "shared" # homozygote overdispersion: "shared" (one value), "locus", "sample" or "locus_sample"
  
  # Inputs for Stan sampling
  stan_iter: 4000 # longer run, mu_error mixes slowly, this brings its Rhat under 1.01
  stan_warmup: 1500
  stan_chains: 4
  stan_adapt_delta: 0.95 # smaller steps, avoids divergences in hierarchical models
  max_error: 0.10 # cap on any error rate, stops "homozygotes" turning into 50/50 heterozygotes

  # Downsampling and genotype confidence calibration
  read_depths_to_test: [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 75]
  draws_per_depth: 300 # random draws per pair and read depth
  minimum_reads_for_truth_pair: 75 # a pair needs at least this many reads, so even the deepest draws are real subsamples
  bootstrap_rounds: 1000 # bootstrap datasets for the confidence bands
---

## Libraries, settings, paths and basic setup 

```{r setup}
suppressMessages({
  library(readxl)
  library(dplyr)
  library(readr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(scales)
  library(parallel)
  library(rstan)
  library(knitr)
  library(bayesplot)
  library(patchwork)
})

# Settings come from the params block in the YAML header, this turns them into usable variables
invisible(list2env(params, envir = environment()))
settings_used <- data.frame(setting = c("run_date", names(params)),
                            value = c(format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"),
                                      vapply(params, function(setting_value) paste(setting_value, collapse = ", "), character(1))))
# Uploading shared functions
source("Code/R_scripts/asp_functions.R", local = TRUE) 

plot_font <- "Times New Roman"
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_family = plot_font))
hm_dark <- "#476F84"
ht_dark <- "#A4552A"
correct_colour <- "#72874E" # correct calls, reads used
error_colour <- "#d73027" # miscalls, incorrect calls, removing cutoffs
group_colours <- c("All pairs" = "grey25", "True homozygotes" = hm_dark, "True heterozygotes" = ht_dark) 


# Folder names are built with a shared function inside asp_functions.R, it gives a unique name based on changed settings for every run. If you use the same settings to rerun it again it gets overwritten. 
run_names <- build_run_names(input_type, use_anchors, anchor_length, threshold_type, error_rate, min_score_fraction,
                             prior_type, prior_het_share, prior_population, prior_floor, probe_type = probe_type,
                             ancestry_prior_shape = ancestry_prior_shape, phi_hom_structure = phi_hom_structure)
output_folder_name_identified <- file.path("Results", dataset_name, "Genotypes_results", run_names$asp_run_name)
stopifnot("ASP results folder not found, run 04_SNP_Genotyping_ASP_primer.Rmd first with the same settings" = dir.exists(output_folder_name_identified))

# primer panel, only locus and the two alleles are needed here (copied from 04, without trimming and anchors)
# the sheet is read once: panel_sheet keeps every column (also the allele frequencies for the HWE prior), panel only the columns needed here
panel_sheet <- read_excel(primer_panel_path, sheet = "Final panel", .name_repair = "minimal")
panel <- panel_sheet[, c("SNP name", "Allele 1", "Allele 2", "ASP1_SEQ (forward allele1)", "ASP2_SEQ (forward allele2)")]
names(panel) <- c("locus", "allele1", "allele2", "asp1_seq", "asp2_seq")
panel <- panel[!is.na(panel$asp1_seq) & !is.na(panel$asp2_seq), ]

timing_log <- list() # empty timing log, log_time() adds one row per step
```


## Hierarchical model for missclasification rate
This chunk contains hierarchical base mixture Bayesian genotyper model for identified Obitools reads, it does one stan call for all samples and loci together. It takes the allele counts for every sample locus pair where k = allele1 reads and d = all usable reads, it doesn't run on reads itself just the genotype deciding process. The naive caller uses a fixed rule for every sample locus pair, if MAF reaches over 20 % the pair is called HT otherwise its HM. Where it lacks is that it treats every locus and sample the same way (I get a results, a specific genotype, but I'm not sure how confident that result is, depth 10 and depth 300 genotypes look the same on the end results heatmap). This Stan model is a bit more sophisticated because it goes around this a different way, it asks "given how noisy this one locus sample pair is, how likely are these allele counts under each genotype?". 
Why use hierarchical? If i want to estimate error rate at each locus i have different ways of computing it on 24 sample and 33 loci. Either with full complete pooling of and treat all loci the same, throw all reads together and compute one global error rate. Its simple, but it lacks nuance. One loci might have a higher error rate because of the homopolymer site right before the SNP position (5 %) and a clean locus could have 0.3 % error rate. One shared value can be too strict or too loose for different loci.
Second option is without pooling and treat every locus separately on its own reads. This option is completely valid, it removes the previous problem but a new one appears. Not all loci have the same amount of depth and data to work with and when there is not a lot of data to work with each estimate relies too much on pure chance.
Third option is partial or hierarchical pooling. It treats each loci separately, but still takes in count that they "come from the same background". Loci are related but not exactly identical (same chemistry, sequencer, pipeline). Each locus gets its own error rate, but those rate are assumed to come from one shared distribution (errors rate is about 3 % but they scatter around by some estimated amount). The model learns both those values, typical error rate  and how much loci really differ (mu_error and sigma_error_locus). Each locus gets its own value but it comes from its own data and the families typical value and that ratio of reliance is based on amount of evidence (depth, number of reads) for each locus separately. Lower depth locus relies more on (is pulled more towards) the typical "family" values, and a locus with more informative reads and higher depth is relies more on its own data. 
The same can happen for samples, one can have a higher error rate because DNA is more degraded. A sample with few reads can borrow from strength from other.
Error rate is calculated as pair error rate =  typical value +  locus effect + sample effect (mu_error + sigma_error_locus * z_error_locus + sigma_error_sample * z_error_sample). Heterozygote allele balance is pooled the same way. its better for genotyping low depth pairs, they can produce overconfident (0 % or 10 %) and extreme estimates and partial pooling pulls it more towards the shared value which makes GQ more meaningful.

Overdispersion: Model handles it in two ways: which DNA molecules happened to be copied and which happened to be sequenced.
A simple binomial model would treat reads for a HT (CT) like coin flips. If every read were an independent "coin flip" from DNA, each read would get a fair chance to be 50 % c or T. The more depth and reads you have, lower the dispersion and closer it is to a true 50 50 split. But reads arent really independent, they come from template molecules, which read get mulitiplied in the PCR is random which affects sequences and reads background. Sequencing more reads or having more depth and data doesnt necessarily give a closer true independent state it just gives a better estimate for that specific split that happened during the labratory prep.
Beta binomial models this with two steps, a true share of copied DNA for specific paris varies at around 50 % (step 1) and the reads are coin flips from that share (step 2). How much step 1 varies is set by phi which can be treated as number of effective templates or molecules. Lower amount of them means more scatter, more of them means it behaves more like  plain binomial. This model fits two of them phi_het for HT with a prior of around 30 molecules and phi_hom and for minor allele reads in HM  with a prior at around 200. With binomials more reads give less scatter, but with betabinomial more reads doesnt neccesarily mean the same thing, scatter levels at around +-9 % because the limit are the molecules not the reads.
Example: HT with 200 reads (140:60 - 30 % for minor) with binomial that is far away from 5050 split (chance of 0.000002%), model would push it towards HM even though that amount of MAF is not typical for HM. With betabinomial that chance is at around  4 %, rare but not almost impossible. Same example but with  20 reads (14:6), binomial gives it 11.5 % and betabinomial 22 %. 
Phi_het also has limits set to at least 10. And its the same for all counts for every sample and locus that is not exactly accurate with reality where low DNA sample has fewer molecules than higher quality DNA sample. Downsampling shows HT are overconfident, for which this one shared phi might be the culprit. Pairs with fewer molecules scatter more than phi allows and the model is too   sure about them. That is why an updated model now uses phi_het separated between samples with the same partial pooling.

Allele bias per locus: in theory two allele specific priors per locus should have the same shares  and are present in equal amounts in HT. In practice those two arent identical, one may bind a little better at the end, that primers specific bindings probabilities can be the cause of the MAF and different split between alleles. This model learns the expected HT split for every locus (het_fraction), its partially pooled across loci like the error rate (a locus with only two HT can claim a strong bias with that little amount of information) and it also has safety limits  het_min and 1 - het_min (0.2 to 0.8). This  can change confident HM calls into less confident HM calls or even HT. A lot of information comes from GQ which gives you confidence on the same scale as Phred

```{r Hierarchical_Stan_Genotyping, eval = params$run_stan}
# Folder name preparation based on previous ASP run and settings used
settings_suffix_hier <- sub("^Identified_ASP_genotypes_", "", run_names$asp_run_name) # same settings label
prior_label_hier <- run_names$prior_label
output_folder_name_hier <- file.path("Results", dataset_name, "Genotypes_results", run_names$bayes_run_name)
dir.create(output_folder_name_hier, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Settings used each run saved directly inside the output folder, useful for reproducibility
write.table(settings_used, file.path(output_folder_name_hier, "settings_used.tsv"), sep = "\t", row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)

# PAth to the stan model, compiled model is saved next to it
stan_model_path_hier <- "Stan_config/base_mixture_model_hierarchical.stan"
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE) 
mixture_stan_hier_model <- stan_model(stan_model_path_hier)

# Reads from the folder not R memory, reads the result files from ASP genotyper pipeline
reads_hier <- read_tsv(file.path(output_folder_name_identified, "all_barcodes_asp_reads.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                       col_types = cols(called_allele = col_character(), called_allele_raw = col_character(), .default = col_guess()))
naive_genotypes_hier <- read_tsv(file.path(output_folder_name_identified, "all_barcodes_asp_genotypes.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                                 col_types = cols(genotype = col_character(), strand_check = col_character(), .default = col_guess()))
cat(sprintf("Stan input: %s (%d reads)\n", run_names$asp_run_name, nrow(reads_hier)))

# Allele counts from the scorer function, only reads that passed every filter
counts_hier <- reads_hier %>%
  filter(!is.na(called_allele)) %>%
  left_join(panel[, c("locus", "allele1", "allele2")], by = "locus") %>%
  group_by(barcode, locus) %>%
  summarise(k = sum(called_allele == allele1),
            d = sum(called_allele == allele1 | called_allele == allele2),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(d >= minimum_required_depth)

# Check that the reads and depth are the same
depth_check_hier <- inner_join(counts_hier, naive_genotypes_hier[, c("barcode", "locus", "depth")], by = c("barcode", "locus"))
stopifnot("reads and genotypes file are from different ASP runs (Stan depth != ASP depth)" = all(depth_check_hier$d == depth_check_hier$depth),
          "the fitted pairs are not the ASP-called pairs" = nrow(counts_hier) == sum(naive_genotypes_hier$status == "called"))

samples_hier <- sort(unique(counts_hier$barcode))
loci_hier <- sort(unique(counts_hier$locus))

# Genotype prior for every locus taken from primer panel when setting is set to "HWE", column taken based on population set
if (prior_type %in% c("hwe", "ancestry")) {
  allele1_frequency_hier <- data.frame(
    locus = panel_sheet[["SNP name"]],
    frequency = as.numeric(panel_sheet[[match(prior_population, names(panel_sheet))]]), # match() takes the first column with this name = allele 1
    dog_frequency = as.numeric(panel_sheet[[match("FreqDOG", names(panel_sheet))]])) # dog side, only used by "ancestry"
}

# This builds the genotype prior for every pair one row per pairs. Prior is chosen from the settings
pair_prior_hier <- switch(prior_type,
  flat = matrix(1/3, nrow = nrow(counts_hier), ncol = 3),
  het_share = matrix(rep(c((1 - prior_het_share) / 2, (1 - prior_het_share) / 2, prior_het_share), each = nrow(counts_hier)), ncol = 3),
  hwe = {
    allele1_p <- allele1_frequency_hier$frequency[match(counts_hier$locus, allele1_frequency_hier$locus)]
    allele1_p <- pmin(pmax(ifelse(is.na(allele1_p), 0.5, allele1_p), prior_floor), 1 - prior_floor) # missing frequency = 0.5, then floored
    cbind(allele1_p^2, (1 - allele1_p)^2, 2 * allele1_p * (1 - allele1_p)) # Hardy-Weinberg: p^2, q^2, 2pq
  },
  ancestry = matrix(1/3, nrow = nrow(counts_hier), ncol = 3)) # placeholder, Stan builds the ancestry prior itself (replaced by the fitted prior after sampling)
colnames(pair_prior_hier) <- c("prior_hom1", "prior_hom2", "prior_het")

# This list is taken by STAN, this is the data that goes into stan model. Everything is turned into number for stan, because it cant use names fro samples or loci
stan_data_hier <- list(
  N = nrow(counts_hier), # number of pairs
  S = length(samples_hier), # number of samples
  L = length(loci_hier), # number of loci
  sample_id = as.integer(factor(counts_hier$barcode, levels = samples_hier)), # Position (indices) of each which sample and locus belongs specific pair
  locus_id = as.integer(factor(counts_hier$locus, levels = loci_hier)),
  k = as.integer(counts_hier$k), # reads for allele 1
  d = as.integer(counts_hier$d), # all filtered reads
  max_error = max_error, # cap on any error rate
  het_min = HT_min_frequence, # heterozygote allele1 fraction stays between 0.2 and 0.8 (1 - HT_minor_frequence)
  pair_prior = unname(pair_prior_hier), # genotype prior for every pair, same order as counts_hier (rows add up to 1), names are removed
  use_ancestry = as.integer(prior_type == "ancestry"), # 1 = Stan learns a wolf ancestry per sample and builds the prior from it
  p_wolf = if (prior_type == "ancestry") pmin(pmax(coalesce(allele1_frequency_hier$frequency[match(loci_hier, allele1_frequency_hier$locus)], 0.5), prior_floor), 1 - prior_floor) else rep(0.5, length(loci_hier)), # per locus in loci_hier order, missing = 0.5, floored
  p_dog = if (prior_type == "ancestry") pmin(pmax(coalesce(allele1_frequency_hier$dog_frequency[match(loci_hier, allele1_frequency_hier$locus)], 0.5), prior_floor), 1 - prior_floor) else rep(0.5, length(loci_hier)),
  ancestry_prior_shape = ancestry_prior_shape,
  phi_hom_by_locus = as.integer(phi_hom_structure %in% c("locus", "locus_sample")), # homozygote overdispersion per locus (partially pooled)
  phi_hom_by_sample = as.integer(phi_hom_structure %in% c("sample", "locus_sample")) # homozygote overdispersion per sample (partially pooled)
)

cat(sprintf("Gathered %d pairs (%d samples x %d loci) - running ONE hierarchical Stan call | genotype prior: %s\n",
            stan_data_hier$N, stan_data_hier$S, stan_data_hier$L, prior_label_hier))

t0 <- Sys.time()

### Actual run for the Bayesian model, finds which parameters fit my data with MCMC sampling and saves all the combinations. results are average of these draws. It runs 4 independent chains with discarded warmup.
fit_hier <- sampling(
  mixture_stan_hier_model, # compiled model from stan file
  data = stan_data_hier,
  iter = stan_iter, warmup = stan_warmup, chains = stan_chains, cores = min(stan_chains, n_cores), 
  control = list(adapt_delta = stan_adapt_delta), # smaller steps, avoids divergences in hierarchical models
  refresh = 0, seed = 1, # no progress messages, same seed for same results when reruning
  pars = "log_genotype_prior", include = FALSE # the per-pair prior is rebuilt in R from wolf_ancestry, not stored for every draw
)
log_time(sprintf("hierarchical sampling: %d pairs", stan_data_hier$N), t0)

# Chain convergence check. Rhat checks if the chains agree (should be at around 1.00, if they disagree > 1.00)- Rhat compares two different spreads within each chain (variations of values inside the chain) and between chains (how far apart the averages are). Rhat should be below 1.01
hyper_pars_hier <- c("mu_error", "sigma_error_locus", "sigma_error_sample", "mu_bias", "sigma_bias", "phi_het", "sigma_phi_het", "phi_hom_typical",
                     if (stan_data_hier$phi_hom_by_locus == 1) "sigma_phi_hom_locus",
                     if (stan_data_hier$phi_hom_by_sample == 1) "sigma_phi_hom_sample") # spreads only when they are estimated
hyper_summary_hier <- summary(fit_hier, pars = hyper_pars_hier)$summary
hyper_labels_hier <- c(mu_error = "Typical error rate (logit scale)",
                       sigma_error_locus = "Error rate spread between loci",
                       sigma_error_sample = "Error rate spread between samples",
                       mu_bias = "Typical heterozygote allele bias (logit scale)",
                       sigma_bias = "Allele bias spread between loci",
                       phi_het = "Effective molecules in heterozygotes (typical sample)",
                       sigma_phi_het = "Effective molecules spread between samples (log scale)",
                       phi_hom_typical = "Homozygote overdispersion (typical pair)",
                       sigma_phi_hom_locus = "Homozygote overdispersion spread between loci (log scale)",
                       sigma_phi_hom_sample = "Homozygote overdispersion spread between samples (log scale)")
kable(data.frame(parameter = hyper_labels_hier[rownames(hyper_summary_hier)],
                 hyper_summary_hier[, c("mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "n_eff", "Rhat")], check.names = FALSE), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

# Grabs the worst Rhat
max_rhat_hier <- max(summary(fit_hier)$summary[, "Rhat"], na.rm = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("Max Rhat: %.3f | divergent transitions: %d | max treedepth hits: %d\n", max_rhat_hier,
            get_num_divergent(fit_hier), get_num_max_treedepth(fit_hier)))

# Extracts all the info about the draws
draws_hier <- extract(fit_hier, c("posterior", "error_locus", "error_sample", "het_fraction", "phi_het", "phi_het_sample", "phi_hom_typical", "phi_hom_pair"))

# Per pair means of all the draws 
post_hier <- apply(draws_hier$posterior, c(2, 3), mean)

# Ancestry prior: the prior of every pair is learned, so the prior columns and the downsampling use its posterior mean (averaged over the draws)
if (prior_type == "ancestry") {
  wolf_ancestry_draws <- extract(fit_hier, "wolf_ancestry")$wolf_ancestry # draws x samples
  allele1_p_draws <- wolf_ancestry_draws[, stan_data_hier$sample_id] * rep(stan_data_hier$p_wolf[stan_data_hier$locus_id] - stan_data_hier$p_dog[stan_data_hier$locus_id], each = nrow(wolf_ancestry_draws)) +
    rep(stan_data_hier$p_dog[stan_data_hier$locus_id], each = nrow(wolf_ancestry_draws)) # q * p_wolf + (1 - q) * p_dog, draws x pairs
  pair_prior_hier <- cbind(prior_hom1 = colMeans(allele1_p_draws^2), prior_hom2 = colMeans((1 - allele1_p_draws)^2), prior_het = colMeans(2 * allele1_p_draws * (1 - allele1_p_draws)))
}

# Parameters for each locus, error rate for average sample and HT allele 1 fraction 
locus_params_hier <- data.frame(
  locus = loci_hier,
  error_rate_locus = round(colMeans(draws_hier$error_locus), 5),
  het_fraction = round(colMeans(draws_hier$het_fraction), 4))

# Parameters for every sample, error rate and and phi_het_sample which are effective starting molecules of the samples HT (for overdispersion)
sample_params_hier <- data.frame(
  barcode = samples_hier,
  error_rate_sample = round(colMeans(draws_hier$error_sample), 5),
  phi_het_sample = round(colMeans(draws_hier$phi_het_sample), 1))

if (prior_type == "ancestry") {
  sample_params_hier$wolf_ancestry <- round(colMeans(wolf_ancestry_draws), 3) # 0 = dog, 1 = wolf
  sample_params_hier$wolf_ancestry_low <- round(apply(wolf_ancestry_draws, 2, quantile, 0.025), 3) # 95 % credible interval
  sample_params_hier$wolf_ancestry_high <- round(apply(wolf_ancestry_draws, 2, quantile, 0.975), 3)
}
  
# This the Rstan results table, one row per fitted pair with info about priors used, posterior porbability for all three genotypes per pair, maximum posterior (genotype) and actual genotype (aa, ct, cc, ...), margin, GQ.
stan_rows_hier <- counts_hier %>%
  left_join(panel[, c("locus", "allele1", "allele2")], by = "locus") %>%
  mutate(
    prior_het = round(pair_prior_hier[, "prior_het"], 4), 
    posterior_hom1 = round(post_hier[, 1], 4),
    posterior_hom2 = round(post_hier[, 2], 4),
    posterior_het = round(post_hier[, 3], 4),
    genotype_key = max.col(post_hier, ties.method = "first"),
    genotype_stan = ifelse(genotype_key == 1, paste0(allele1, allele1),
                    ifelse(genotype_key == 2, paste0(allele2, allele2),
                           paste0(pmin(allele1, allele2), pmax(allele1, allele2)))), # Alphabeticaly sorted
    max_posterior = round(apply(post_hier, 1, max), 4),
    margin = round(apply(post_hier, 1, function(p) diff(sort(p, decreasing = TRUE)[2:1])), 4),
    GQ = round(pmin(99, -10 * log10(pmax(1 - apply(post_hier, 1, max), 1e-10))), 1)
  ) %>%
  select(barcode, locus, k, genotype_stan, prior_het, posterior_hom1, posterior_hom2, posterior_het, max_posterior, margin, GQ)

# Combined table for both runs, the naive one and Bayes, with strand check and QD, depth aswell.
combined_genotypes_hier <- naive_genotypes_hier %>%
  select(barcode, locus, genotype_naive = genotype, depth, status, strand_check, QD) %>%
  left_join(stan_rows_hier, by = c("barcode", "locus")) %>%
  left_join(locus_params_hier, by = "locus") %>%
  left_join(sample_params_hier, by = "barcode") %>%
  mutate(
    genotype = ifelse(genotype_stan != genotype_naive & strand_check %in% "failed" & # final genotype change when strand check si true
                        substr(genotype_stan, 1, 1) != substr(genotype_stan, 2, 2),
                      genotype_naive, genotype_stan), 
    changed = !is.na(genotype_naive) & !is.na(genotype) & genotype_naive != genotype
  ) %>%
  select(barcode, locus, genotype, genotype_stan, genotype_naive, depth, k, status, strand_check, QD,
                prior_het, posterior_hom1, posterior_hom2, posterior_het, max_posterior, margin, GQ,
                error_rate_locus, error_rate_sample, phi_het_sample, het_fraction, changed)

# Final results table writing per sample
for (id in unique(combined_genotypes_hier$barcode)) {
  write_tsv(combined_genotypes_hier %>% filter(barcode == id),
            file.path(output_folder_name_hier, paste0(id, "_base_mixture_genotypes_hierarchical.tsv")))
}

# Convergence table, all the parameters summary
```
